title: Researchers stretch LeCun's JEPA AI into a universal world model that works from physics to biology
key_facts: A team led by PhAI Labs with researchers from Stanford, Oxford and Princeton introduced JEPA-Anything, an extension of Yann LeCun's JEPA architecture.
JEPA models predict an abstract summary of a missing or future state rather than raw data; JEPA-Anything splits the prediction into several modules that are pushed to capture different aspects.
Against a standard JEPA under identical conditions, prediction error fell 35% in a simplified Pong test with interventions and 13% for unseen combinations of interventions.
It beat the baseline across ten tasks spanning physics, robotics and weather, according to the authors; gains were small on image tasks and the baseline won one of three robot-walking environments.
The model's top liver-cancer candidate paired IL-18 with CD73 blockade; in organoids and tissue from three patients and in mice it killed more tumour cells than either alone.
The study does not establish whether this could become a therapy.
Trained on simulated orbits, it recovered Kepler's third law with an exponent of -1.4991 against the true -1.5, from one chosen training run.
Code and models are publicly available.
quote_evidence: The study doesn't establish whether this could become an actual therapy.
The team only evaluated one training run, and picked the one with the lowest error.
Clean separation of the learned parts doesn't mean they capture real cause-and-effect relationships, the authors caution.
why_it_matters_hint: A single method works across many sciences, but results are early and the cancer finding is lab-stage only.
notes: Authors' own results; no outside review mentioned.
